content_html:
Future value is what money you have today, plus money you add along the way, will be worth at a set date once interest or growth has been applied. It is one half of the time value of money: a dollar invested now becomes more than a dollar later. This calculator handles both parts of a typical plan, a single starting amount and a stream of equal deposits, and shows how much of the final figure each part contributes.

How to use this calculator

  1. Starting amount: the lump sum you have now, also called the present value. Enter 0 if you are only making deposits.
  2. Deposit each period and frequency: the regular amount you add and how often, from weekly to yearly.
  3. Annual interest rate and years: the stated yearly rate and how long the money grows. Partial years are allowed.
  4. Deposit timing: deposits at the end of each period form an ordinary annuity; deposits at the start form an annuity due and earn one extra period of interest each.
  5. More options: set a compounding schedule that differs from your deposits, or raise each year's deposits by a fixed percentage.

The future value formula

The calculator first turns the annual rate into a rate for each deposit period, i. When interest compounds as often as you deposit, that is simply the annual rate divided by the number of deposits a year. Then:

FV = PV × (1 + i)n + PMT × [(1 + i)n − 1] ÷ i

Here PV is the starting amount, PMT the deposit, and n the number of deposits. The first term is the lump sum growing on its own; the second adds up every deposit, each growing for the time left after it is made. For deposits at the start of each period, the second term is multiplied by (1 + i). If the compounding schedule is different, the period rate becomes (1 + r/m)m/p − 1, where m is compounding periods and p deposits per year.

Worked example

Start with $1,000 and deposit $100 at the end of every month for 10 years at 6% compounded monthly. The monthly rate is 0.5% and there are 120 deposits.

PartCalculationValue after 10 years
Starting amount$1,000 × 1.005120$1,819.40
Monthly deposits$100 × (1.005120 − 1) ÷ 0.005$16,387.93
Future valueSum of both$18,207.33

You put in $13,000 in total, so $5,207.33 is interest. Moving the same deposits to the start of each month raises the result to $18,289.27.

Practical tips

  • Use the effective annual rate shown in the results to compare accounts that compound differently.
  • Run the numbers at a few rates rather than one, especially for investments where returns are not fixed.
  • A yearly deposit increase is a simple way to model saving more as your income grows.
  • The result is in future dollars. Inflation will reduce what that amount can buy, so discount it with a present value or inflation calculator if you want today's purchasing power.

faq.question: What is the difference between future value and present value?
faq.answer: Future value moves money forward in time by adding growth, while present value moves a future amount back to today by removing growth. They use the same rate and number of periods, just in opposite directions.

faq.question: Should I choose deposits at the start or the end of each period?
faq.answer: Choose the start if you deposit as soon as each period begins, such as on payday at the start of the month. Choose the end if you deposit after the period closes. Start-of-period deposits produce a slightly higher future value because each one earns an extra period of interest.

faq.question: Can the future value be lower than the money I put in?
faq.answer: Not with this calculator, because rates are limited to 0% or higher. At 0% the future value equals the starting amount plus all deposits. A real investment can lose value, which a fixed-rate projection does not show.

faq.question: Why does compounding frequency change the answer only a little?
faq.answer: More frequent compounding credits interest sooner, so interest starts earning interest a bit earlier. At typical rates the gap between monthly and daily compounding is small; the rate itself and the number of years have a much larger effect.

faq.question: Does this include taxes or account fees?
faq.answer: No. The figures are before tax and fees. If an account charges a yearly fee, you can approximate it by lowering the interest rate by the fee percentage.
